strengths: Addresses important and practical problem in computational science with substantial empirical improvements (up to 100× reduction in high-fidelity simulations)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse tasks with appropriate metrics (C2ST, NLTP) and good validation practices (simulation-based calibration, posterior predictive checks)
Well-executed studies with extensive implementation details and multiple method variants (amortized, sequential, active learning) demonstrating generality of the approach
Consistent improvements shown across different problem characteristics and parameter space dimensionalities
Pragmatic handling of real implementation challenges (parameter dimension mismatch, leakage, numerical stability)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward transfer learning (pre-train on low-fidelity, fine-tune on high-fidelity) applied to NPE without significant algorithmic innovation

Critical dependence on low-fidelity model quality is under-explored: no systematic ablations on sensitivity to LF model misspecification or degradation; no guidance for practitioners on constructing/validating LF models

Missing critical baseline comparisons: no comparison with other multifidelity SBI methods (Prescott & Baker 2020/2021); no ablation showing marginal benefit of transfer learning specifically vs. sequential inference alone (MF-TSNPE vs. TSNPE)
Unclear how much improvement comes from multifidelity vs. sequential nature: MF-TSNPE substantially outperforms amortized MF-NPE, but the isolated contribution of transfer learning is unknown

Limited guidance on applicability and scalability: inherited NPE/TSNPE limitations for high-dimensional parameters acknowledged but not addressed; no principled framework for when this method is suitable; largest task has 24 HF parameters (12 in LF) without convincing scalability demonstration

Model misspecification robustness insufficiently tested: dummy variable approach for parameter mismatch is heuristic and shows performance degradation; no experiments with intentionally misspecified LF models

Missing ablation studies: sensitivity to number of LF vs. HF simulations; cost-benefit analysis (when does pre-training become justified?); comparison of transfer learning vs. simpler pre-training alternatives
Acquisition function in A-MF-TSNPE shows only minor improvements despite higher computational cost; no diagnosis of why acquisition function is ineffective or exploration of alternatives

Construction of low-fidelity models is domain-specific with no generalizable framework: all three tasks have naturally available simplifications (compartment reduction, mean-field theory, i.i.d. Gaussian) that may not generalize to new problems

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine computational bottleneck in SBI with expensive simulators
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse tasks with rigorous statistics (10 network initializations, confidence intervals, calibration checks)
Consistent empirical improvements demonstrating 1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in required high-fidelity simulations
Clear presentation of experimental setup with detailed hyperparameters and prior specifications in appendices
Methodologically sound approach with appropriate evaluation metrics (C2ST, NLTP) and baselines
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contribution is straightforward application of standard transfer learning (pre-train/fine-tune) to NPE, lacking novel algorithmic or theoretical insights
Weak theoretical justification: Paper provides no rigorous analysis of why/when features should transfer between low- and high-fidelity simulators beyond hand-wavy 'feature space overlap' claims

Unprincipled handling of parameter dimension mismatch via dummy variables: When low-fidelity has fewer parameters, authors feed noise for exclusive dimensions; authors acknowledge this is suboptimal but offer no principled alternative

Missing critical experimental comparisons: No comparison to multifidelity ABC methods (Prescott & Baker 2020, 2021; Warne et al. 2022) or ROPE despite citing them; unclear why neural density estimation advantage holds

Inadequate characterization of applicability: Paper acknowledges effectiveness depends on simulator similarity but provides no quantification, sensitivity analysis to model mismatch, or systematic failure case study
Limited multifidelity scenarios: Experiments use architectural simplifications (fewer compartments) or same-model variants rather than truly independent simulators, raising generalizability questions
Unfair baseline comparison: MF-NPE uses both low- and high-fidelity data while NPE uses only high-fidelity, conflating effects of total training data with transfer benefits

Sequential method contributions minimal: MF-TSNPE is straightforward application of transfer to existing TSNPE; A-MF-TSNPE shows only marginal improvements despite ensemble overhead and unresolved posterior leakage issues
No practical guidance for practitioners: Paper provides no principled method for choosing amount of low-fidelity data or determining when investment in low-fidelity model is worthwhile
Missing key ablations: No study of weight freezing effects, architecture sensitivity, low-fidelity data amount optimization, or performance with intentionally mismatched simulators
Scalability limitations: Maximum 24 parameters demonstrated; modern SBI handles higher dimensions; paper acknowledges high-dimensional limitations without addressing them
Model misspecification section superficial: Section 2.3 introduces connection but doesn't deeply integrate or provide novel insights beyond citing existing work

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem in simulation-based inference with clear practical motivation and impact (100x reduction in high-fidelity simulations demonstrated)
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse tasks (analytical benchmark and two real neuroscience simulators) with appropriate metrics (C2ST, NLTP, simulation-based calibration)
Clear and well-written presentation with informative visualizations, detailed algorithms, and extensive supplementary material for reproducibility
Solid technical execution of transfer learning approach with sensible extensions to sequential methods (MF-TSNPE) and active learning (A-MF-TSNPE)
Consistent empirical improvements across all tasks with confidence intervals and posterior predictive checks validating quality
Fair evaluation protocol testing on high-fidelity observations with parameters from prior
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: transfer learning through pre-training is standard ML practice; application to multifidelity SBI is incremental rather than methodologically innovative

Critical missing baseline comparisons: paper only compares to NPE baseline and does not compare to existing multifidelity SBI methods mentioned in related work (Prescott & Baker 2020, 2021; Warne et al. 2022; Prescott et al. 2024), making it impossible to assess competitive positioning

Ad-hoc parameter dimension mismatch handling via dummy variables leads to pre-trained estimator estimating prior for high-fidelity-only parameters; acknowledged as suboptimal with no principled solution

Insufficient exploration of failure modes: critical limitation that 'effectiveness relies on similarity between low and high-fidelity models' is relegated to Discussion; no systematic study of degradation as fidelity gap increases

Acquisition function (A-MF-TSNPE) analysis is superficial: shows only minor improvements while requiring expensive ensemble training; proposes biased sampling without correction, relying on empirical results without theoretical justification

Missing computational cost analysis: reports high-fidelity simulation reductions but no total wall-clock time comparisons; training costs for low-fidelity pre-training not quantified; overhead relative to benefits unclear
Incomplete sequential method evaluation: MF-TSNPE (5 rounds) vs. amortized MF-NPE fundamentally different; no comparison to TSNPE baseline; computational accounting unclear

Restricted scope and applicability: requires manual domain expertise to construct low-fidelity models (not automated); two of three real tasks are neuroscience simulators; no exploration of multiple fidelity levels

Hyperparameter and design choices under-explored: network architecture fixed without ablation; early stopping criterion S never clearly specified; transformations (logit, z-scoring) chosen without justification; limited sensitivity analysis
No theoretical justification for when/why transfer learning should help in this setting beyond citing empirical transfer learning literature

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: computational expense of high-fidelity simulators in scientific inference
Comprehensive experimental validation across six diverse tasks with multiple metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE)
Two non-trivial real-world neuroscience applications (multicompartmental neuron, spiking networks) demonstrating practical value
Thorough empirical analysis including investigation of when pre-training helps (mutual information and representational coherence), simulation-based calibration, and computational cost comparisons
Demonstrates substantial simulation efficiency gains (up to 100x reduction in high-fidelity simulations needed)
Clear presentation with detailed algorithms, reproducibility information, and promised code release
Proper handling of parameter space mismatches between fidelities and multiple network initializations for robustness
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of standard transfer learning (fine-tuning) to NPE; incremental methodological advance with concurrent work pursuing similar ideas
Lacks theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or formal characterization of when/why transfer learning helps for multifidelity posteriors

Incomplete investigation of critical limitations: dependence on low-fidelity model quality, parameter space mismatch handling via dummy variables is somewhat ad-hoc, A-MF-TSNPE shows inconsistent improvements and adds significant overhead
Experimental evaluation only on high-fidelity observations; real empirical data with model mismatch would strengthen claims about practical utility
MF-ABC comparison weakened by authors' acknowledgment that more extensive hyperparameter search could substantially improve MF-ABC performance

Limited scalability analysis and practical guidance: maximum parameter dimension tested is 24; unclear when simulation cost justifies training overhead; A-MF-TSNPE requires expensive ensemble training

Insufficient exploration of transfer learning mechanism: why features from low-fidelity generalize to high-fidelity not clearly characterized; no analysis of negative transfer scenarios or failure modes

strengths: Addresses practical problem of expensive simulators in Bayesian inference
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 benchmarks and 2 real neuroscience applications with multiple evaluation metrics
Real-world neuroscience applications (L5PC neurons, spiking networks) demonstrate utility with domain-derived low-fidelity models
Analysis of transfer learning conditions via mutual information and representational similarity (Section 4.4)
Extensive supplementary material with detailed experimental specifications
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: standard transfer learning applied to NPE; concurrent work (Thiele et al., Hikida et al., Saoulis et al. 2025) developing similar approaches without comparison
No theoretical analysis: explicitly acknowledges inability to provide convergence guarantees or formal characterization of when transfer learning helps in NPE setting
Critical evaluation gap: total computational cost evaluated only on 2 of 6 tasks; claims of 'two orders of magnitude' reduction are misleading without accounting for low-fidelity simulation overhead
Narrow applicability: method depends on availability of good low-fidelity models; limited guidance on design or identification; performance degrades when parameter spaces differ (OU4 case)
Inconsistent improvements: modest on benchmarks with A-MF-TSNPE showing no significant benefit on 2/3 tasks; strongest where researchers hand-designed low-fidelity models
Weak baseline comparisons: no comparison to other SBI efficiency techniques (Dyer et al., Schmitt et al., Delaunoy et al.) or concurrent multifidelity work
Underdeveloped transfer learning methodology: simple weight initialization without exploring architectural choices, layer freezing, or domain adaptation techniques
Table 4 reveals training costs can rival or exceed simulation savings in some regimes, undermining practical advantage claims

strengths: Addresses genuine practical problem (expensive simulators in SBI) with clear motivation
Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation with 4 benchmarks + 2 real neuroscience applications, multiple metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE), proper baselines (NPE, TSNPE, MF-ABC)
Significant empirical results showing consistent 50-100× reduction in high-fidelity simulations needed across diverse tasks
Methodologically complete: handles amortized and sequential variants, different parameter dimensionalities, multiple fidelities
Insightful analysis of transfer learning effectiveness via controlled experiments identifying mutual information and representational coherence as key factors (Appendix B)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, task descriptions, promised code release, multiple independent runs
Clear presentation with effective figures and logical organization
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is applying standard transfer learning (fine-tuning) to NPE, a straightforward combination of existing techniques; multifidelity itself is well-established in optimization/UQ
Concurrent work by Saoulis et al. (2025) independently applies transfer learning to multifidelity SBI, significantly reducing novelty claims

Lacks theoretical understanding: no formal analysis of why transfer learning helps in NPE; claim that pre-trained features 'overlap' (Section 3.1.1) is intuitive but unjustified; Appendix B acknowledges current theoretical frameworks rely on simplifying assumptions not applicable here

Strong assumptions limiting applicability: requires similarity between low/high-fidelity models (acknowledged Section 5), assumes negligible low-fidelity cost, depends on high mutual information between simulators (Appendix B shows sharp performance drops when MI is low)

Incomplete empirical analysis: saturation effect observed (no improvement between 10^4-10^5 LF samples) with no guidance on sample count selection; total cost analysis deferred to appendix for benchmarks; A-MF-TSNPE overhead substantial (557s training) with marginal improvements over MF-TSNPE in some tasks (SIR, SLCP); mixed sequential results unexplained
Scalability limitations not addressed: method inherits NPE's issues with high-dimensional parameter spaces; multifidelity approach doesn't solve this fundamental limitation
Algorithm simplicity (Algorithm 1: just weight initialization) combined with limited theoretical justification raises questions about contribution depth
Limited failure mode analysis: unclear when pre-training might hurt; what if low-fidelity model is adversarially different? Appendix B explores when transfer helps but not failure cases

Evaluation metric concerns: C2ST requires true posterior samples (rarely available in practice); NLTP can be circular; different evaluation protocols across tasks (30 vs 10 observations, different seeds) complicate comparison
Missing practical guidance: no clear decision rules for when to use MF-NPE vs standard NPE; no principled approach to choosing low-fidelity sample budget given fixed total budget
